questions.q: Why does this lesson build one KQL query with the whole IOC list templated into a `dynamic([...])` array, instead of looping one lookup per IOC?
options: One round trip checked against every IOC at once scales far better than a few thousand separate API calls for a feed with a few thousand indicators
dynamic([...]) arrays can only hold a single value at a time
A watchlist must be queried before any KQL query can run
KQL does not support loops, so a loop in Python is the only option regardless of IOC count
questions.explain: A let statement with a dynamic([...]) array is KQL's parameterized IN clause — one query covers the whole IOC list instead of one round trip per indicator.

questions.q: Why does the lesson introduce a chunked() generator before building large KQL queries?
options: To randomize the order of IOCs for security reasons
Because KQL queries have a practical length ceiling, and a dynamic([...]) array built from tens of thousands of IOCs can exceed it
Because the Sentinel API requires IOCs to be submitted in alphabetical order
Because Python dictionaries cannot hold more than 5000 keys
questions.explain: Chunking splits a large IOC list into batches (e.g. 5000 at a time) so each generated query stays under KQL's length limit.

questions.q: What does bulk_upsert_watchlist() do, and why does the lesson prefer bulk/batched calls over a tight loop of synchronous single-item PUT requests?
options: It deletes the entire watchlist and rebuilds it from a CSV file, which is the only way Sentinel supports updates
It keeps a standing watchlist current so analytics rules can reference it; batching respects the API's throttling limits instead of hammering it with thousands of rapid-fire calls
It only works for domains, never for IP addresses or file hashes
It converts the watchlist into a STIX bundle for export to another SIEM
questions.explain: The watchlist API accepts bulk create-or-update operations; batching calls (rather than one synchronous PUT per item in a tight loop) is the throttling-respectful approach a DevSecOps review would expect.

questions.q: After running the KQL lookup, what does the "seen_in_environment" vs. "not_observed" tag actually represent?
options: Whether the IOC's confidence score from the feed was above or below 50
Whether the IOC was pulled from a STIX/TAXII feed versus a CSV feed
Whether the IOC is an IP address versus a domain name
Whether the IOC actually matched real log data (SourceIP/DestinationIP) in CommonSecurityLog, as opposed to merely appearing on a threat feed with no corroborating activity
questions.explain: The tag separates "this IOC exists in a feed" from "this IOC actually touched our environment" — a distinction Lesson 15's scoring pass relies on heavily.

questions.q: Which client/library does this lesson reuse from the Chapter 2 Sentinel-scripting material to run the templated KQL query?
options: The taxii2-client library used for pulling STIX/TAXII feeds
A raw socket connection to the Log Analytics workspace
LogsQueryClient from azure-monitor-query, authenticated with DefaultAzureCredential
The Microsoft Graph Security API client from Chapter 2's lesson on Graph fundamentals
questions.explain: The same LogsQueryClient from azure-monitor-query, authenticated via DefaultAzureCredential, is reused here — now templated with an IOC list instead of a fixed query string.
